license: Our own (story text written for Waymark)

data.title: Embers
data.intro: The Signal Tower has been dark for forty winters. Its beacon once answered ships, caravans and storms; now pigeons nest in the lantern room. The Guildmaster hands you a pair of brass headphones. “The tower doesn’t need eyes,” she says. “It needs ears. Every sound you learn lights a lamp on the stair. Light enough of them, and the beacon may remember how to speak.”

trial.name: The Gatekeeper
trial.text: The stair narrows at an iron gate. Behind it, a voice in the static sends without pause and never repeats. Copy 50 characters at 90% or better and the gate will open.

data.outro: The gate swings open onto the upper stair. For the first time in forty winters, a faint glow shows in the lantern room, and down in the square, people stop to look up.

data.text: The first lamp on the stair takes the flame. Somewhere below, old wiring hums awake.
A second lamp. The Guildmaster doesn’t look up from her ledger. “Two sounds. Everyone starts with two.”
Dust lifts from the steps as the third lamp wakes. On the landing lies the last operator’s logbook, its final entry unfinished.
The fourth lamp shows a brass key on the sill, warm, as if someone had only just set it down.
The shortest sound of all, and the brightest lamp yet. The pigeons leave the lantern room.
Six lamps. Out on the water, a fishing boat flashes its deck light at the tower. Coincidence, surely.
The seventh lamp lights a door marked RADIO ROOM. It is locked from the inside.
Eight lamps burn on the stair. The Guildmaster closes her ledger. “The Gatekeeper will want a word with you.”

data.title: The Upper Stair
data.intro: Above the gate the stair turns cold and narrow. The logbook speaks of “the far voice”: a station that kept calling the tower long after it went dark.

trial.name: The Warden of the Stair
trial.text: The Warden sends faster than the Gatekeeper and mixes every sound you know. Copy 50 characters at 90% or better.

data.outro: The second gate opens. The lantern room is close now, and somewhere in the static you are sure you heard someone call the tower by name.

data.text: The ninth lamp, and a draught from a broken pane. You stop the gap with a page from the logbook’s empty back.
The tenth lamp. The next page of the logbook is dated the night the beacon failed.
Lamp eleven shows a callsign scratched into the rail, half worn away by forty winters of hands.
Twelve lamps. Music drifts up from the Caravanserai; the city keeps later hours now that the tower glows.
The thirteenth lamp. In a hurried hand, the logbook says: “The far voice is getting weaker. I will answer tomorrow.”
The full stop lights the fourteenth lamp. Sentences can end now, and so can messages.
Lamp fifteen. The locked radio room hums whenever you pass its door.
Sixteen lamps. At the top of the stair waits a second gate, older than the first, with a speaking grille.

data.title: The Lantern Room
data.intro: Beyond the second gate, a ladder climbs into the lantern room. The great lens is cracked and gray with salt, and beside it sits the last operator’s chair, turned toward the window as if waiting.

trial.name: The Keeper of the Lens
trial.text: The lens will not turn for a stranger. Its keeper sends in long, even lines, and now numbers too. Copy 50 characters at 90% or better.

data.outro: The lens turns a quarter-turn on its old bearings and catches the evening light. Out on the water, three boats answer at once.

data.text: A break sign lights the seventeenth lamp: the pause between one thought and the next. The logbook uses it on every page.
Lamp eighteen. The operator’s chair creaks as you pass, though nobody is in it.
Nineteen lamps. The cracked lens throws their light in pieces across the walls.
The twentieth lamp. Taped inside the logbook’s cover: a list of stations the tower once spoke to, most of them crossed out.
A comma for the twenty-first lamp. Messages can breathe now.
Lamp twenty-two. The window glass hums when the wind comes off the sea, like a carrier with nobody on it.
Twenty-three lamps. The Guildmaster climbs up to see for herself, and stays longer than she meant to.
The first number, and the twenty-fourth lamp. The logbook’s last pages are full of them: times, bearings, signal strengths.

data.title: The Far Voice
data.intro: With the lens turning, the tower can listen farther than ever. Each night, at the same hour, something faint comes through the static: the far voice from the logbook, still calling.

trial.name: The Storm Front
trial.text: A storm rolls in and the far voice comes through it in pieces. Copy 50 characters at 90% or better, numbers and signs included.

data.outro: The storm passes. In the quiet after it, the far voice sends one clear line: the tower’s own callsign, and then a question mark.

data.text: A slash for lamp twenty-five. It splits callsigns from where they’re sent: the far voice is somewhere else tonight.
The twenty-sixth lamp. Q means a question in the operator’s shorthand, and the logbook is full of them.
Lamp twenty-seven. You write down the hour the far voice comes: always nine minutes past.
Twenty-eight lamps. The far voice sends two letters, again and again. They might be initials.
The twenty-ninth lamp. Down in the square, the night watch has taken to looking up at the tower when it chimes.
Lamp thirty. The logbook’s author signed off with “73”: best regards, in the old shorthand.
Thirty-one lamps. The far voice is stronger tonight. Someone is turning toward you, too.
The thirty-second lamp. The radio room door is warm to the touch, and its lock has rusted through.

data.title: The Beacon Speaks
data.intro: One flight of stair is left in the dark, and with it the last sounds an operator needs. When they’re lit, the beacon can answer whoever is calling.

trial.name: The Beacon’s Answer
trial.text: To relight the beacon, you must copy everything it will ever need to say: every letter, number and sign you know, at full pace. Copy 50 characters at 90% or better.

data.outro: The beacon blazes. Its light sweeps the water and the square, and from the radio room comes a clear, steady signal: the far voice, answering at last. The radio room door swings open. Inside, a chair, a key and a headset wait for an operator ready to hold a conversation.

data.text: A question mark for lamp thirty-three, the sign the far voice ends with every night.
Thirty-four lamps. A child in the square points at the tower and counts them out loud.
Lamp thirty-five. You can send “73” yourself now, the operator’s goodbye.
The thirty-sixth lamp. Its light reaches the Caravanserai’s courtyard, and a toast is raised to the tower.
Thirty-seven lamps. In the logbook’s last entry, a single number: one more night.
Lamp thirty-eight. The lens turns a full circle for the first time in forty winters.
The thirty-ninth lamp. The Guildmaster brings two cups of tea and sits in the empty chair beside you.
Forty lamps, the zero with the long, slow sound. The whole stair burns now, from the gate to the lantern room.
The last lamp. Every sound the tower knows is yours. The beacon waits for its answer.
